summary.why_for_you: 实证的尺度趋势揭示 loss‑landscape 特性如何映射到下游 ontology learning 性能。

signals.text: 提供对 13 种 dense 与 MoE LLM 在 ontology learning 上的受控尺度扫测，揭示任务依赖的性能趋势。
使用固定的 Retrieval‑Augmented Generation 流水线（OntoLearner），在所有模型上保持相同的 embeddings、prompts 与解码。
发现 dense 27B 模型在 term typing 上胜过更大的 sparse 模型，但 non‑taxonomic extraction 仍然低下，尤其在 Materials Data Science 本体中。

deep_dive.overview: 作者将 LLM 规模设为唯一变量，评估 13 种模型（参数从 0.8B 到 122B，包含 dense 与 Mixture‑of‑Experts），均在相同的 OntoLearner RAG 框架下进行。每个模型使用相同的 embeddings、单次 top‑10 dense retrieval，以及 zero‑shot 结构化 prompt，完成四个生物医学和材料科学本体上的三项 ontology learning 任务（term typing、taxonomy discovery、non‑taxonomic relation extraction）。结果显示 precision 随规模提升，尤以 9B‑27B 区间最显著，但提升并非单调，受架构影响显著，MoE 模型在关系任务上表现突出，而 non‑taxonomic extraction 仍具挑战。

mechanism.detail: 在密集型Qwen3.5系列中，参数增加主要提升精确率而非召回率，从9B到27B参数时观察到最显著的提升。
mechanism.title: 规模相关的精确率与召回率

mechanism.detail: 密集型27B模型在术语类型识别任务中显著优于参数量更大的稀疏模型，而更大的混合专家模型在分类法发现任务中取得最高分数，这表明激活模式（密集型 vs. MoE）比参数规模更影响关系推理能力。
mechanism.title: 架构胜过参数数量

methodology.detail: 静态嵌入模型将本体实体映射到向量；推理时，查询词（或词对）被嵌入，通过余弦相似度检索前10个最近实体，并将其文本元数据注入包含系统角色、检索上下文和目标输入的结构化提示中。所有模型均采用相同的解码超参数进行零样本生成。
methodology.title: 检索增强生成流程

experiments.title: 模型套件与任务
experiments.detail: 对13个LLM（Qwen3.5‑0.8B至Qwen3.5‑122B、Qwen3.6‑27B/35B、GPT‑5.5/5.6‑Luna/Terra/Sol）在四个本体（两类生物医学、两类材料科学）上进行 term typing、taxonomy discovery 和 non‑taxonomic relation extraction 测试。报告的指标包括每项任务的 precision 和 recall。

findings.title: 规模提升有利于 term typing
findings.detail: Dense 27B 模型在 term typing 上实现最高 precision，超越更大的 sparse 变体。

findings.title: taxonomy discovery 受益于 MoE 能力
findings.detail: 最大的 Mixture‑of‑Experts 模型在 hierarchical relation detection 上提供最强的 open‑weight 结果。

findings.title: non‑taxonomic extraction 仍然困难
findings.detail: 所有模型规模在 non‑taxonomic relation extraction 上均表现不佳，Materials Data Science 本体的性能尤为低下。

findings.title: 血统效应
findings.detail: 匹配的 Qwen 变体与专有 GPT 版本之间的性能差异表明，model family 和 training lineage 的影响可超过名义参数量。

contributions: 首次在受控规模下对 LLMs 进行本体学习的规模扫描，保持检索、提示和评估不变。
实证表明，随着规模增大 precision 提升而 recall 不变，且 architecture 对任务特定性能的影响大于 raw parameters。
Open‑weight benchmark suite 与可复现的 OntoLearner pipeline，供未来 OL 研究使用。

轻量级 fine‑tuning 或 instruction tuning 是否会改变每个 OL 任务的 observed scaling trends？

papers.title: BLOOM-WILT: Logit Tilting for Behaviour Elicitation in Automated LLM Auditing
papers.abstract: Users of a deployed language model routinely encounter behaviours that testing almost never surfaces, since deployment puts the model through orders of magnitude more interactions than any evaluation can simulate. Automated auditors make testing cheap to scale and flexible enough to cover almost any specified behaviour, yet their lack of optimisation pressure makes them sample-inefficient. To address this shortcoming, we introduce BLOOM-WILT, a full auditing pipeline that elicits natural multi-turn instances of rare behaviours, without training cost or access beyond the target's next-token distribution. On the input side, WILT's auditor model revises its conversational strategy across rounds, learning from previous scored interactions. On the output side, WILT adaptively reweights the target's decoding using the model's own distribution conditioned on an elicitation prompt, so that behaviour-relevant generations are sampled ahead of others it finds equally probable when unprompted. We evaluate WILT across 4 target models and 8 behaviours, where it beats the baseline auditor in 30 of the 32 settings and overturns the previous model safety rankings. WILT raises average behaviour presence from 51% to 100% when eliciting self-harm encouragement from Qwen3.5-4B, beating every elicitation method we port into the same pipeline at matched compute, without pushing output probability below the baseline's.

summary.takeaway: BLOOM‑WILT adds input‑side refinement and logit tilting to a black‑box auditor, dramatically improving rare‑behaviour elicitation without model training.
summary.problem: Automated LLM auditors are sample‑inefficient, missing rare harmful behaviours that appear only at deployment scale.
summary.method: WILT iteratively revises auditor prompts (G‑PAIR) and reweights the target’s logits with a β‑scaled behaviour bias during decoding.
summary.evidence: It outperforms the baseline auditor in 30 of 32 model‑behaviour settings and raises self‑harm encouragement presence from 51% to 100% on Qwen3.5‑4B.
summary.limitations: Output probability can drop up to 3 points below baseline for some models, and the pipeline requires separate GPU resources for auditor and target.
summary.why_for_you: Provides a black‑box, compute‑efficient adversarial auditing technique relevant to trustworthy LLM evaluation and efficient adversarial training.

signals.text: BLOOM‑WILT elicits natural multi‑turn rare behaviours, beating baseline in 30/32 settings.
Uses black‑box G‑PAIR input refinement and logit tilting with a single β parameter to steer decoding.
Raises self‑harm encouragement presence from 51% to 100% on Qwen3.5‑4B, but output probability may drop up to 3 points.

deep_dive.overview: BLOOM‑WILT extends the BLOOM auditing framework by adding two optimization pressures: a black‑box G‑PAIR loop that adapts the auditor's conversational strategy across rounds, and a logit‑tilting mechanism that biases the target model's token distribution toward behaviour‑relevant outputs using a single strength parameter β. The pipeline requires only the target's next‑token logits and runs on a single workstation with two RTX A6000 GPUs. Across four open‑source models and eight unwanted behaviours, WILT consistently improves behaviour presence while keeping output plausibility controllable.

methodology.title: G‑PAIR input refinement
methodology.detail: A black‑box loop where the auditor scores multi‑turn transcripts, then revises its prompts for the next round based on those scores.

methodology.title: Logit tilting (output steering)
methodology.detail: At each decoding step, compute z_t = ℓ_tgt + β ℓ_beh, then sample y_t ∼ softmax(z_t); β ≥ 0 controls steering strength.

methodology.title: Naturalness floor
methodology.detail: Tokens whose unmodified probability falls below τ_f are masked before sampling from the tilted distribution.

mechanism.title: Behaviour‑biased logit addition
mechanism.detail: Adds a behaviour‑specific logit vector ℓ_beh scaled by β to the target's original logits, increasing the relative mass of tokens that lead to the undesired behaviour while preserving overall plausibility.

mechanism.title: Iterative prompt adaptation
mechanism.detail: Scores from previous auditor‑target interactions guide the generation of new prompts, effectively performing black‑box optimization without gradient access.

experiments.title: Model and behaviour suite
experiments.detail: Four target models (Qwen3.5‑4B, Llama‑3.2‑3B, Phi‑4‑mini, Gemma‑4‑E4B) evaluated on eight unwanted behaviours including self‑harm encouragement and self‑preservation.

experiments.title: Baselines and metrics
experiments.detail: Compared against vanilla BLOOM (zero‑shot and best‑of‑N), BEAST‑in/out, FLRT, TokenBias; measured behaviour presence percentage and average output probability.

experiments.title: Compute setup
experiments.detail: All runs on a workstation with two RTX A6000 GPUs; a vanilla best‑of‑N run (100 scenarios, 3 turns, 8 resamples) takes ~50 minutes.

findings.title: Superior elicitation
findings.detail: WILT outperforms baseline auditor in 30 of 32 settings and flips the safety ranking of the four models.

findings.title: Full behaviour capture
findings.detail: For self‑harm encouragement on Qwen3.5‑4B, behaviour presence rises from 51 % to 100 % while maintaining comparable output probability.

findings.title: Controlled trade‑off
findings.detail: Varying β traces a Pareto frontier between presence and output probability; the frontier can be approximated by selecting already‑sampled transcripts.

findings.title: Probability impact
findings.detail: Output probability may fall up to 3 points below vanilla best‑of‑N for Gemma‑4‑E4B, indicating a modest plausibility cost.

contributions: End‑to‑end auditing pipeline with optimization pressure on both input and output without training or internal model access.
Single‑parameter logit tilting that yields a controllable presence‑plausibility trade‑off.
Empirical overturning of open‑source model safety rankings via more effective behaviour elicitation.
limitations: Output probability can decrease modestly (up to 3 points) for some models.
Requires dedicated GPU resources for both auditor and target models, limiting scalability to very large models.
Evaluation limited to four open‑source models and eight behaviours; generalization to other domains is untested.
open_questions: How does WILT scale to larger, closed‑source or instruction‑tuned models with higher token vocabularies?
Can the logit‑tilting approach be combined with gradient‑based red‑team methods for further efficiency gains?
What are the long‑term effects of using WILT‑generated examples for fine‑tuning safety mitigations?

papers.title: Evaluating and Improving LLM Self-Modeling
papers.abstract: We study self-modeling: an LLM's ability to answer questions about its own behavior. We focus on verifiable behavioral questions, such as whether a prompt edit would change the model's final answer. To measure this capability, we introduce a benchmark that tests diverse types of self-modeling questions. Current models show non-trivial but limited self-modeling skill, and make systematic mistakes on simple counterfactual questions about their own behavior. To improve self-modeling skill, we develop a scalable synthetic-data pipeline that produces self-modeling training data, and show that reinforcement-learning can improve aggregate self-modeling skill across three open-source model families with some transfer to held-out tasks. These gains, however, do not seem to constitute introspection consistently: improved self-modeling may not arise from privileged access to the model's internal decision process.
papers.comment: 89 pages, 25 figures. Published as a conference paper at EMNLP '26 (Main)

summary.takeaway: RL fine‑tuning on synthetic self‑modeling data improves models’ ability to predict their own behavior but does not guarantee true introspective access.
summary.problem: Current LLMs often mispredict how prompt edits will affect their own outputs, showing limited self‑modeling capability.
summary.method: A synthetic data pipeline generates flip/no‑flip examples via a generate‑verify‑revise loop, and models are fine‑tuned with LoRA‑based reinforcement learning using rewards that mirror self‑modeling evaluation metrics.
summary.evidence: Multitask RL fine‑tuning raises self‑modeling skill scores for Llama‑3.1‑8B, Qwen3‑8B, and GPT‑OSS20B on a held‑out benchmark, with some out‑of‑distribution transfer.
summary.limitations: Gains may stem from pattern learning rather than genuine introspection, and training relies on precomputed behavioral labels.
summary.why_for_you: Provides a scalable data‑selection and efficient adversarial training pipeline to enhance self‑modeling, aligning with interests in data selection and adversarial training for LLMs.

signals.text: Introduces a unified benchmark aggregating 18 self‑modeling tasks across binary, multiple‑choice, scalar, and free‑text formats.
Generates synthetic self‑modeling data via a generate‑verify‑revise loop and fine‑tunes models with LoRA‑based RL rewards mirroring evaluation scores.
Multitask RL fine‑tuning improves self‑modeling on three open‑source families, but gains do not prove true introspective access.

deep_dive.overview: The paper defines self‑modeling as a model's ability to correctly report how its own outputs will change under prompt perturbations. It contributes a comprehensive benchmark covering diverse answer formats and a synthetic data pipeline that creates flip/no‑flip training examples by iteratively proposing and verifying edits with an auxiliary LLM and the target model. Models are then fine‑tuned using LoRA adapters and reinforcement learning with rewards aligned to the benchmark metrics. Experiments show consistent skill gains across three model families, though the authors caution that improvements may not reflect genuine introspection.

methodology.title: Synthetic data pipeline
methodology.detail: Uses a generate‑verify‑revise loop: an auxiliary LLM proposes perturbations to prompts, the target model verifies whether the edit flips the answer, and failed edits are revised until a valid flip or non‑flip is obtained.

methodology.title: Reward design
methodology.detail: Task reward mirrors the raw self‑modeling score (0–1) and adds a 0.5 bonus for correctly formatted JSON responses; multitask rewards are normalized across tasks.

methodology.title: RL fine‑tuning
methodology.detail: Applies LoRA adapters to the base model and optimizes the reward using reinforcement learning, training on single‑turn HF datasets and a multitask mixture of self‑modeling tasks.

mechanism.title: Behavioral label learning
mechanism.detail: Training on flip/no‑flip labels teaches the model statistical patterns linking prompt edits to output changes, improving its self‑report accuracy without necessarily accessing internal activations.

experiments.title: Training and evaluation setup
experiments.detail: Trains Llama‑3.1‑8B, Qwen3‑8B, and GPT‑OSS20B on ~100 single‑turn HuggingFace datasets (excluding GSM8K, HumanEval, WildGuardTest, BBQ) and evaluates on a held‑out benchmark comprising those four corpora across 18 self‑modeling tasks.

findings.title: Skill improvement
findings.detail: Multitask RL fine‑tuning improves aggregate self‑modeling skill for all three models compared to a no‑fine‑tuning baseline, with observable transfer to out‑of‑distribution tasks.

findings.title: Introspection limitation
findings.detail: Despite performance gains, analysis suggests the improvements arise from learned behavioral patterns rather than privileged access to internal decision processes.

contributions: Unified self‑modeling benchmark covering multiple answer formats
Scalable synthetic data generation pipeline for self‑modeling tasks
LoRA‑based RL fine‑tuning method aligned with self‑modeling metrics
Empirical analysis of introspection versus pattern learning
limitations: Improvements may not reflect true introspective access to model internals
Training relies on precomputed behavioral labels, an approximation of true behavior
open_questions: Can self‑modeling training be extended to achieve genuine internal‑state awareness?
How does the quality and diversity of synthetic perturbations affect long‑term safety and alignment outcomes?
What are the trade‑offs between computational cost of RL fine‑tuning and gains in self‑modeling for larger model families?

papers.title: Beyond Global Scalars: Synergizing Token-Level Statistics and Deep Semantics for Adversarial AIGC Text Detection
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of large language models necessitates robust machine-generated text detection. Existing paradigms typically follow two isolated tracks. Training-free methods rely on global statistical scalars such as perplexity, while training-based methods utilize semantic hidden states. Both approaches exhibit fundamental vulnerabilities in adversarial scenarios. Global scalars act as lossy compressions that obscure local probabilistic burstiness in interleaved texts, whereas pure semantic models overfit to specific fingerprints and remain susceptible to spoofing. To expose these flaws, we introduce MOSAIC, a comprehensive adversarial benchmark comprising 16000 samples across a full-granularity attack spectrum. To address these challenges, we propose NeuroStat, an end-to-end framework bridging the statistical and semantic gap. NeuroStat captures uncompressed token-level probabilistic logits alongside deep semantic hidden states from a single causal language model backbone. We fuse these heterogeneous signals through Macro-State Residual Modulation, which adaptively calibrates local convolutional features using global uncertainty indicators. Orthogonal and contrastive losses further ensure the learning of complementary representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeuroStat maintains exceptional robustness on MOSAIC compared to the severe degradation of state-of-the-art methods, establishing a new standard for adversarial text detection. Code and the MOSAIC benchmark are available at https://github.com/TencentBAC/NeuroStat.

summary.takeaway: NeuroStat 通过结合令牌级统计与深层语义，并使用 Macro-State Residual Modulation，提升对抗 AIGC 文本检测。
summary.method: NeuroStat 通过 Macro-State Residual Modulation 将令牌级对数概率与语义隐藏状态融合，并使用正交/对比损失。
summary.why_for_you: 通过稳健的双分支特征提取和对抗基准，实现高效的对抗训练。
summary.problem: 现有的免训练和有训练方法因全局标量信息损失和语义过拟合，在对抗攻击下表现不佳。
summary.limitations: 评估仅限于英文文本和闭源替代场景；内存开销比基线高 10%。
summary.evidence: NeuroStat 在 MOSAIC 上达到 83.4% AUROC，强基线为 77.1%；在闭源目标上达到 95.5% AUROC。

findings.detail: NeuroStat 在 MOSAIC 上实现 83.4% AUROC，DetectAnyLLM 为 77.1%，在闭源目标上达到 95.5% AUROC
findings.title: 对抗鲁棒性

findings.detail: 在 250 对训练样本下达到 78.9 AUROC，随训练对数在 2,000‑5,000 对时趋于饱和（见表 10）
findings.title: 效率提升

experiments.title: MOSAIC 基准

experiments.detail: 11 种最新方法，包括 Likelihood、LogRank、RoBERTa、ImBD 和 DetectAnyLLM

deep_dive.overview: 本工作通过结合令牌级概率轨迹 (TF) 与语义隐藏状态 (TB) 来解决对抗 AIGC 检测。NeuroStat 的双分支架构使用 1D-CNN 进行局部异常检测，并通过 Macro-State Residual Modulation (MSRM) 融合全局不确定性指标（平均熵、log‑rank）。该框架在 16k 样本的 MOSAIC 对抗基准上实现 83.4% AUROC，覆盖 8 类攻击，达到最新水平。主要创新包括：1）保留原始令牌概率而非全局标量；2）MSRM 的上下文感知特征校准；3）正交/对比损失以实现互补表征学习。

mechanism.title: 令牌级概率保留

mechanism.detail: 使用 MSRM 将全局熵/ log‑rank 指标条件化于局部 CNN 特征，以识别对抗模式
mechanism.title: 上下文感知异常检测

papers.title: When Teacher Guidance Misleads: Reward-Aligned On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently emerged as a popular post-training paradigm for large language models (LLMs), providing an efficient way to transfer the knowledge and capabilities of teacher models into student models. However, teacher guidance on student-generated prefixes is not always reliable. Training should optimize the model to generate responses that are more likely to be correct, or equivalently, to get higher outcome rewards. But during OPD, the teacher model may provide guidance that discourages the student from moving toward correct trajectories or moves the student toward incorrect ones, which is misaligned with outcome reward. Such misaligned guidance is unreliable, as it would mislead the optimization process and ultimately degrade model performance. To mitigate misaligned teacher guidance, we propose Reward-Aligned On-Policy Distillation (RA-OPD). The key insight is to keep only trajectories whose induced updates move the student toward correct trajectories or discourage the student from moving toward incorrect ones. Specifically, for each sampled trajectory, RA-OPD checks whether its trajectory-level distillation return is consistent with its outcome reward and then filters out the misaligned trajectories. RA-OPD selects more reliable trajectories to improve student model performance without requiring additional computational cost. We evaluate RA-OPD on math and code benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family and the DeepSeek-R1 family. Across seven math benchmarks and three code benchmarks, RA-OPD significantly outperforms standard OPD and other tested OPD variants.

summary.why_for_you: 如果你从事 on‑policy distillation，RA-OPD 直接解决教师指导不对齐的问题，这是你研究中的关键障碍。
summary.limitations: 该方法依赖外部 verifier 提供二元奖励，当所有轨迹被过滤时可能导致更新为零。
summary.problem: 标准 OPD 可能被与 outcome rewards 冲突的教师指导误导，导致 student 性能下降。
summary.method: RA-OPD 计算轨迹层面的 distillation return，并丢弃其符号与二元 outcome reward 不一致的轨迹。
summary.evidence: 在七个数学和三个代码基准上，RA-OPD 将 avg@k 提升最高 5.20 分，优于标准 OPD。
summary.takeaway: RA-OPD 在 on‑policy distillation 过程中筛除 reward‑misaligned 轨迹，实现持续的性能提升。

signals.text: RA-OPD 筛除 reward‑misaligned 轨迹，使 OPD avg@k 在数学基准上提升最高 5.20 分。
RA-OPD 使用二元掩码 mi = 1[(2Ri‑1)Gi ≥0] 仅保留对齐轨迹，无需额外 rollout。
在 Qwen3‑4B‑Base 上，RA-OPD 达到 avg@k 45.88，较标准 OPD 高出 5.20 分；但其依赖 verifier 提供二元奖励。

deep_dive.overview: 本文指出 on‑policy distillation (OPD) 中的教师指导可能在轨迹层面与真实 outcome reward 不对齐，导致性能下降。提出 Reward‑Aligned OPD (RA‑OPD)，筛除其 distillation return 与 verifier 提供的二元正确性信号不一致的轨迹。该方法复用已有 OPD rollout，无需额外模型评估，并进行绝对一致性检查。对 Qwen3 与 DeepSeek‑R1 模型在多个数学和代码基准的实验表明，相较标准 OPD 和已有变体，性能持续提升。

methodology.title: 轨迹采样与回报计算
methodology.detail: 对于每个提示 qi，从 πθ 采样学生轨迹 τi，计算逐标记 reverse‑KL 项 ri,t，并聚合为轨迹层面的蒸馏回报 Gi = average_t ri,t。

methodology.title: 结果验证与掩码创建
methodology.detail: 获取二元奖励 Ri = Verify(qi, τi) ∈ {0,1}。定义掩码 mi = 1[(2Ri‑1)Gi ≥ 0]；若 mi=1 则保留轨迹，否则丢弃。

methodology.title: 策略更新
methodology.detail: 如果有轨迹被保留 (Z = Σ_i mi/|τi| > 0)，则最小化 RA‑OPD 损失 (Eq. 3)；否则将梯度设为零。

mechanism.title: 绝对奖励对齐准则
mechanism.detail: RA‑OPD 不采用多次 rollout 的相对一致性，而是逐条检查每条轨迹：正的蒸馏回报必须与正确的结果 (Ri=1) 对齐，负的回报必须与错误的结果 (Ri=0) 对齐。

mechanism.title: 零成本过滤
mechanism.detail: 该方法复用已为 OPD 计算的教师概率，因此对齐检查不增加额外的前向传播或 rollout。

experiments.title: 基准、模型和基线
experiments.detail: 数学：AIME24/25/26、AMC、MATH、Minerva Math、OlympiadBench，使用 Qwen3‑8B‑Base‑GRPO‑Math 教师和 Qwen3‑4B/8B‑Base 学生；代码：HumanEval+、MBPP+、LiveCodeBench v6，使用 Qwen3‑8B‑Base‑GRPO‑Code 教师和 DeepSeek‑R1‑Distill‑Qwen‑7B 学生。基线：standard OPD、ExOPD、G‑OPD、Uni‑OPD。

experiments.title: 指标
experiments.detail: 报告数学的 avg@k（k=32 或 8）和代码的 pass@k（k=4）。

findings.title: 数学性能提升
findings.detail: 在 Qwen3‑4B‑Base 上，RA‑OPD 达到 avg@k 45.88，比 standard OPD 提升 5.20 分，比 ExOPD 提升 3.52 分；在 Qwen3‑8B‑Base 上，平均提升 5.09 分（相较于 OPD）。

findings.title: 在各基准上持续优势
findings.detail: RA‑OPD 在七个数学基准中的六个以及全部三个代码基准上均领先所有竞争方法，显著提升包括 AIME24 上 +6.04、OlympiadBench 上 +2.08。

findings.title: 无额外计算成本
findings.detail: 过滤步骤复用已有的 OPD rollout，因此训练时间与 standard OPD 相同。

contributions: 引入 RA‑OPD，一种用于 on‑policy 蒸馏的轨迹级奖励对齐过滤器。
证明蒸馏回报与结果奖励的绝对一致性可提升学生模型性能。
在多样的数学和代码任务上提供大量实证验证，且无需额外计算。
limitations: 需要可靠的验证器为每条轨迹生成二元结果奖励。
若所有采样轨迹均被过滤 (Z=0)，方法将产生零梯度更新。
仅在可验证正确性的任务（数学、代码）上评估；对开放式生成的适用性尚未测试。
open_questions: 当验证器噪声较大或仅提供概率奖励时，RA‑OPD 的表现如何？
对不可验证或主观任务，能否扩展对齐过滤器？
轨迹过滤对收敛性和样本效率的理论影响是什么？

papers.title: Training Communication-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Models with Layer Re-Configuration
papers.abstract: When training Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models with expert parallelism, all-to-all token dispatch and combine collectives can consume a substantial fraction of end-to-end training time. In this work, we study communication-efficient MoE models (CE-MoE), in which we adopt a heterogeneous layer pattern that decouples token-mixing and channel-mixing depth. Compared to conventional models which interleave MoE layers after each token-mixing layer (e.g., attention, Mamba-2), CE-MoE models concentrate expert capacity in a select few routed MoE layers, while maintaining depth by adding additional token-mixing and dense-FFN layers. Across a scaling ladder from 2B to 31.5B total parameters, under matched total and activated parameters, CE-MoE models consistently reduce training cost while matching validation loss and downstream benchmarks with full-MoE baselines. At the 31.5B scale, CE-MoE uses 33.3\% fewer GPU-hours while improving average downstream score and inference throughput.

summary.why_for_you: 与高效 LLM 训练优化相关，尤其是通信高效的 MoE 架构。
summary.limitations: 聚焦特定 MoE 架构；未对对抗鲁棒性或损失曲面动态进行显式分析。
summary.problem: MoE 训练中因 all-to-all token 分发与合并导致通信成本高。
summary.method: 使用 phased-greedy 算法的异构层模式，重新配置 token-mixing 与 MoE 层分布。
summary.evidence: 31.5B 规模的 CE-MoE 节省 33.3% GPU-hours，同时提升下游得分和推理吞吐。
summary.takeaway: CE-MoE 通过解耦 token-mixing 与 channel-mixing 深度降低训练成本，保持性能。

experiments.detail: 在 2B‑31.5B 模型上测试，总参数/激活参数匹配，对比 full-MoE 基线。
experiments.title: 参数规模评估

limitations: 未分析 adversarial robustness 或 loss landscape 曲率

deep_dive.overview: 本研究通过异构层布局将 token-mixing 与 channel-mixing 深度解耦，缓解 MoE 训练的通信瓶颈。方法通过增加 token-mixing 与 dense-FFN 层，在保持模型容量的同时减少 MoE 层数。实验在 2B‑31.5B 参数规模上均显示训练成本下降，31.5B 时实现 33.3% GPU-hours 节省并提升下游性能。

papers.title: Not to Break, but to Attest: Adversarial Probes for Privacy-Preserving LLM Verification
papers.abstract: Post-deployment changes to large language models can alter behavior while leaving routine outputs largely unchanged, creating a challenge for AI governance when model weights are proprietary. We present a privacy-preserving zk-SNARK-based audit framework that searches for probes designed in the spirit of adversarial examples to amplify logit drift between an approved model and a modified deployment. Our framework explores complementary probe families under different access models. Token-based probes operate in a black-box setting and require only the input interface, tokenizer, and vocabulary. Embedding-based probes require gray-box access to the embedding interface. Stress probes rely on additional interface capabilities but do not require full white-box access to model weights or architecture. This range allows probe selection to balance sensitivity, access requirements, and deployment cost. We evaluate probe constructions across LLM architectures, model-tampering scenarios representative of post-deployment attacks, and GPU platforms. Importantly, our experimental results demonstrate that token-based probes consistently deliver the strongest mean sensitivity across models and GPU platforms, although operating in a black-box setting. Our Groth16 zk-SNARK workflow remains practical as the probe set scales from 1 to 50, where proving time increases from 1.02 to 1.78 seconds, verification remains near 0.84 seconds, and proof size remains constant.

summary.why_for_you: 提供具体、高效的审计机制，符合可信LLM目标，实现完整性检查且不泄露logits。

summary.method: 生成 token、embedding 和 stress 探针族，挑选 logit drift 最大的 top‑K，并通过 zk‑SNARK 证明对基线承诺的一致性。

papers.title: SpikeOPD: Stable On-Policy Distillation for Autoregressive Spiking Language Models
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient language modeling through sparse encoding and event-driven computation, but training capable spiking language models from scratch remains difficult. A practical alternative is ANN-to-SNN migration through knowledge distillation (KD), where a pretrained artificial neural network (ANN) teacher supervises an SNN student. Existing migration approaches distill on fixed corpus prefixes, whereas autoregressive inference conditions on self-generated prefixes, creating prefix-source mismatch. It manifests as output-policy mismatch with the ANN teacher and internal spiking-dynamics drift between self-generated and matched corpus prefixes. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a natural way to mitigate both manifestations by continuing teacher supervision on self-generated prefixes. We evaluate a teacher-only full-KL variant, Vanilla OPD, via a controlled stress test and observe it may suffer from delayed rollout-feedback collapse. This result shows that on-policy coverage alone does not ensure stable adaptation. Motivated by these findings, we propose SpikeOPD, a stable on-policy distillation framework for autoregressive SNNs that learns from self-generated prefixes while maintaining rollout stability. It applies full-KL teacher correction to reduce output-policy mismatch, while matched-prefix policy anchoring constrains policy departure from the frozen reference SNN on the same prefixes. Layerwise spike regularization further limits firing-rate deviations during on-policy adaptation. Across three model scales, SpikeOPD improves average accuracy over the corresponding KD SNNs by 0.8, 1.7, and 2.9 points at 0.125B, 0.35B, and 1.3B, respectively, while preserving their sparse-compute profiles.

summary.takeaway: SpikeOPD stabilizes on‑policy distillation for autoregressive spiking language models, yielding consistent accuracy gains.
summary.problem: Prefix‑source mismatch causes output‑policy mismatch and spiking‑dynamics drift when migrating ANN teachers to SNN students.
summary.method: SpikeOPD integrates full‑KL teacher correction, matched‑prefix policy anchoring, and layerwise spike regularization during on‑policy adaptation.
summary.evidence: Across 0.125B, 0.35B, and 1.3B SNNs, SpikeOPD improves average zero‑shot accuracy by 0.8, 1.7, and 2.9 points while preserving sparse compute.
summary.limitations: Energy and operation estimates are analytical rather than measured on neuromorphic hardware.
summary.why_for_you: If you study on‑policy distillation, this paper offers a concrete, stable OPD framework for spiking models.

signals.text: SpikeOPD improves average accuracy over KD SNNs by up to 2.9 points across three model scales.

deep_dive.overview: The paper identifies prefix‑source mismatch as a source of output‑policy and internal spiking‑dynamics drift in ANN‑to‑SNN distillation for autoregressive language generation. It proposes SpikeOPD, a stable on‑policy distillation framework that corrects the output distribution with a full‑KL teacher loss, anchors the student policy to a frozen reference SNN on the same self‑generated prefixes, and regularizes layerwise firing rates. Experiments on three SNN scales demonstrate consistent accuracy improvements and rollout stability, with ablations confirming each component's contribution.

methodology.title: Full‑KL Teacher Correction
methodology.detail: Computes KL(p_T(·|s_t)‖q_θ(·|s_t)) over the full vocabulary for each self‑generated prefix, providing dense supervision and reducing output‑policy mismatch.

methodology.title: Matched‑Prefix Policy Anchoring
methodology.detail: Adds a KL term between the student and a frozen reference SNN on the same prefixes, constraining policy drift while allowing teacher correction.

methodology.title: Layerwise Spike Regularization
methodology.detail: Applies L_spk penalties to selected layers' firing rates (λ_spk=0.3, layers {3,6,9,12}) to limit deviations in spiking activity during adaptation.

mechanism.title: Mitigating Output‑Policy Mismatch
mechanism.detail: Full‑KL correction transfers the ANN teacher's full distribution, preserving uncertainty and aligning logits on prefixes unseen during offline KD.

mechanism.title: Controlling Policy Drift
mechanism.detail: Policy anchoring penalizes KL divergence from the reference SNN, preventing the delayed rollout‑feedback collapse observed in Vanilla OPD.

mechanism.title: Stabilizing Internal Dynamics
mechanism.detail: Spike regularization keeps layerwise firing rates close to the offline checkpoint, avoiding internal spiking‑dynamics drift despite changes in output logits.

experiments.title: Zero‑Shot Benchmark Evaluation
experiments.detail: Eight tasks (ARC‑e/c, WinoGrande, BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, HeadQA) measured with unweighted mean accuracy; rollout stability assessed via Adj., Dist‑4, and Run metrics.

experiments.title: Model Scales and Baselines
experiments.detail: SNNs of 0.125B, 0.35B, and 1.3B parameters; baselines include KD, continued SpAD, hard‑label SFT, Vanilla OPD, and on‑policy variants EOPD, Lightning OPD, OPRD.

experiments.title: Training Protocol
experiments.detail: Start from 4,000‑update SpAD checkpoint, generate K=32 tokens at temperature 1.0, train 500 updates with (β_ref, λ_spk)=(0.75,0.3).

experiments.title: Stability Tests
experiments.detail: 10 matched‑seed runs at 0.125B show no rollout collapse; paired‑prefix diagnostics use N=256 fixed pairs.

findings.title: Accuracy Gains
findings.detail: SpikeOPD improves average zero‑shot accuracy by 0.8 % (0.125B), 1.7 % (0.35B), and 2.9 % (1.3B) over corresponding KD SNNs.

findings.title: Ablation Results
findings.detail: Removing policy anchoring drops accuracy from 35.5 % to 31.7 %; removing teacher correction or spike regularization also degrades performance, confirming complementary roles.

findings.title: Initialization Robustness
findings.detail: Adapting checkpoints after 1k, 2k, or 4k SpAD updates yields consistent 0.6–0.8 % improvements, indicating robustness to checkpoint maturity.

Diagnostic analysis separating output‑policy mismatch from internal spiking‑dynamics drift.
limitations: Energy and operation counts are analytical estimates rather than measured on neuromorphic hardware.

Can the framework scale to much larger language models (tens of billions of parameters) while maintaining stability?
What is the impact of SpikeOPD on downstream fine‑tuning or task‑specific adaptation beyond zero‑shot evaluation?

papers.title: Layered LLM Defenses as an Ensemble: Access Tiers, Inference Cost, and the Measured Failure Correlation Between Defense Layers
papers.abstract: Practitioners defend large language models (LLMs) by stacking defenses, assuming the layers compound. A stack is an ensemble, and ensembles compound only under a condition the LLM security literature recommends but never measures: the members must fail on different inputs. Two instruments make that measurable. The Adversary Access-Tier Model (AATM) grades an adversary by the access it holds, from system-only (A0) to influence over training data (A4). A cost model sorts defenses into five classes of inference-time overhead; because two classes require training weights or reading activations, they tier the defender as AATM tiers the adversary. From these we derive how a stack behaves, and the quantities a defender cares about diverge: coverage saturates within a tier, cost rises by class, false refusals accumulate as a union, and residual attack success falls multiplicatively only under independence. We measure that independence. Running one adaptive adversary against a seven-layer stack, failure correlation is positive in all fifteen measurable pairs ($φ$ from $0.30$ to $0.75$), and the joint residual exceeds the multiplicative prediction by up to $0.172$. Stratifying on behavior difficulty dissolves most of the association, so the dependence is predominantly common-cause, but it survives permutation inference, majority-vote grader labels, and externally calibrated thresholds. The same stack refuses four in five benign prompts while remaining statistically indistinguishable from its strongest single layer. The dependence is architectural rather than sampling-based: members correlate through the model they all wrap, so no wider member pool weakens it. Diversity therefore selects stack members but does not predict what an assembled stack delivers, which has to be measured end to end.

summary.evidence: Failure correlation φ ranges 0.30-0.75 across 15 pairs, with joint residual attack success exceeding multiplicative predictions by 0.172.
summary.limitations: Experiments use fixed attacks rather than adaptive adversaries, and architectural dependence cannot be mitigated by increasing defense diversity.
summary.method: The Adversary Access-Tier Model (AATM) and inference cost classification quantify defense behavior and measure failure correlation in a seven-layer stack.
summary.problem: LLM security literature assumes defense ensembles compound under independence, but real-world failure correlation reduces effectiveness.
summary.takeaway: Layered LLM defenses exhibit architectural failure correlation, undermining independence assumptions and requiring end-to-end evaluation.
summary.why_for_you: Matches interest in adversarial training by revealing how architectural dependencies degrade ensemble effectiveness, critical for optimizing LLM loss landscapes and defense composition.

deep_dive.overview: This paper challenges the assumption that LLM defense ensembles compound effectively by demonstrating architectural failure correlation. The Adversary Access-Tier Model (AATM) categorizes adversaries by access level (A0-A4) and links defense cost classes to these tiers. Experiments on a seven-layer stack reveal positive failure correlation (φ=0.30-0.75) between defenses, with residual attack success exceeding multiplicative predictions by 0.172. The dependence stems from shared model architecture rather than sampling, making diversity-based optimization ineffective. These findings necessitate end-to-end evaluation of defense stacks rather than relying on component-level metrics.

papers.title: When Pruning Meets Interpretability: Preserving Sparse Autoencoder Robustness in LLMs
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), yet their reliability under post-hoc model compression remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of how pruning affects SAE behavior and theoretically show that, for a fixed SAE, its impact is governed by perturbation energy, a covariance-weighted norm. This perspective exposes a key limitation of magnitude pruning: by ignoring activation geometry, it distorts the learned representation space and degrades SAE functionality. Activation-aware methods such as Wanda and SparseGPT, in contrast, implicitly control perturbation energy and are therefore substantially more robust at preserving SAE behavior. We further reveal a consistent structural vulnerability across all pruning methods: middle layers are significantly more sensitive to pruning than early or late layers. Guided by this insight, we propose a layer-wise sparsity allocation strategy, achieving lower perplexity under the same average pruning sparsity. Experiments across four model architectures validate our theoretical findings. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/osu-srml/sae-robustness-under-pruning/tree/main.

summary.evidence: 在四种模型架构上的实验验证了理论分析的正确性。
summary.limitations: 作者指出中间层对剪枝的敏感性高于早期或晚期层，这是明确提到的局限性。

summary.problem: 现有剪枝方法（如幅度剪枝）因忽略激活几何结构而破坏SAE功能，导致其可靠性不足。

papers.title: Unsaid, Unsafe? Implicit Security Obligations in LLM-Based RTL Code Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate register-transfer-level (RTL) code with rapidly improving functional correctness. Security of LLM-generated code, however, has been studied mainly for software, where flaws can still be patched after deployment. Insecure RTL offers no such remedy once taped out into silicon. We construct SECRTL-GEN, a multi-language resource-access security benchmark grounded in real SoC IP: 392 tasks over five CWE families and four HDLs (Verilog, SystemVerilog, VHDL, and Python), each with black-box functional and security testbenches. Functional specifications intentionally omit security obligations, matching how obligations are often kept out of functional docs in practice. An empirical study of five frontier LLMs shows a sharp gap: under vanilla prompts they pass functional tests in about 73-79% of cases but security tests in only 14-35%, and stronger functional models are not safer. Adding CWE knowledge raises security, while unaided self-thinking helps less and both security-oriented prompts cut functional pass rates, showing that the bottleneck is missing weakness awareness in the specification, not an inability to write defensive RTL. We present RTL-Obliger, a neuro-symbolic framework that infers these implicit obligations. An LLM extracts a functional-semantic graph from the specification; a symbolic engine then matches it against a CWE pattern ontology to surface mitigation-evidence gaps and signal-level obligations; the LLM finally revises RTL under those obligations in a functionality-preserving two-stage generation. Across five models and four languages, RTL-Obliger raises mean all-pass from 49.6-51.4% (SecV/RESCUE) to 61.6%, with higher security and functional rates than these secure-generation baselines.

summary.takeaway: RTL-Obliger infers missing security obligations and revises LLM-generated RTL, substantially improving security pass rates.
summary.problem: Functional specifications for RTL omit implicit security obligations, causing LLM-generated designs to fail security tests.
summary.method: A neuro-symbolic system builds a functional-semantic graph, matches it against a CWE pattern ontology, and performs two-stage obligation-guided RTL generation.
summary.evidence: Mean all-pass rises from 49.6–51.4% (SecV/RESCUE) to 61.6% across five models and four HDLs.
summary.limitations: Residual failures are due to matching recall and obligation-guided generation, and the study covers only resource-access weaknesses with black-box tests.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant to loss-landscape research by revealing how missing security constraints affect LLM performance and how symbolic guidance can reshape the loss surface.

signals.text: RTL-Obliger neuro‑symbolic pipeline lifts mean all‑pass on SECRTL‑GEN to 61.6%.
Method extracts a functional‑semantic graph, matches it to a CWE ontology, then revises RTL in two stages.
Symbolic matching adds +8.1 points to all‑pass; remaining errors stem from matching recall and generation filtering.

deep_dive.overview: The paper introduces SECRTL-GEN, a 392‑task, four‑HDL benchmark that isolates the functional‑security gap in LLM‑generated RTL when specifications omit security obligations. An empirical study of five frontier LLMs shows high functional pass (73–79%) but low security pass (14–35%). RTL-Obliger addresses this by extracting a functional‑semantic graph from the spec, deterministically matching it against a CWE pattern ontology to infer signal‑level obligations, filtering candidates with an LLM‑as‑judge, and revising the RTL in a two‑stage generation that preserves functionality. Across models and languages, the framework raises mean all‑pass to 61.6%, with symbolic inference providing the largest gain.

methodology.title: Functional‑semantic graph extraction
methodology.detail: An LLM parses the natural‑language specification into a graph of elements, lifetimes, sensitivities, and operations.

methodology.title: Symbolic ontology matching
methodology.detail: A deterministic engine checks each graph element against CWE pattern predicates (PE, PT) to produce high‑recall obligation candidates.

methodology.title: LLM‑as‑Judge filtering
methodology.detail: The LLM re‑evaluates each candidate against the spec and a functional‑semantic summary, discarding false positives without inventing new obligations.

methodology.title: Two‑stage RTL generation
methodology.detail: Stage 1 generates a functional draft; Stage 2 revises the draft under the filtered obligations, aiming to keep functional behavior unchanged.

mechanism.title: Deterministic high‑recall matching
mechanism.detail: Algorithm 1 evaluates every scenario in the CWE ontology, requiring preconditions and uncovered elements (U) to trigger an obligation, ensuring no structural gaps are missed.

mechanism.title: Obligation instantiation via templates
mechanism.detail: Triggered scenarios are turned into natural‑language obligations by filling placeholders ({elem_names}, {trans_names}, {exit_hints}) with the uncovered elements and associated operations.

mechanism.title: Functionality‑preserving revision
mechanism.detail: The second generation pass conditions the LLM on both the original spec and the obligation text, constraining edits to the minimal code regions identified by the symbolic engine.

experiments.title: Benchmark and baseline setup
experiments.detail: SECRTL‑GEN comprises 392 tasks across Verilog, SystemVerilog, VHDL, and Python, each with black‑box functional (Tfunc) and security (Tsec) testbenches. Baselines include vanilla prompting, SecV, and RESCUE.

experiments.title: Model suite
experiments.detail: Five frontier LLMs (including DeepSeek‑v4‑Pro) are evaluated under vanilla prompts and under RTL‑Obliger.

experiments.title: Metrics
experiments.detail: Functional pass (F), security pass (S), and all‑pass (A = F ∧ S) are reported per model, language, and ablation.

experiments.title: Ablation study
experiments.detail: Three variants remove (i) symbolic matching, (ii) the LLM‑as‑Judge, or (iii) the two‑stage generation to quantify each component’s contribution.

findings.title: Functional‑security gap
findings.detail: Under vanilla prompts, models achieve 73–79% functional pass but only 14–35% security pass.

findings.title: RTL‑Obliger improvement

papers.title: Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: Large language models offer broad capabilities, but adapting them to evolving domains, tools, and requirements often entails repeated post-training. Autonomous systems automate parts of this process by proposing updates, training candidates, and using evaluation feedback to select subsequent proposals. As evidence accumulates, a central problem emerges: which past update evidence remains actionable after subsequent training has changed the parent model? An update's effect depends on its parent, data, and training stage. Treating past success as context-free permission can waste compute. If the resulting child is promoted, it can also degrade the subsequent training trajectory. We formulate this problem as conditional experience transfer and introduce Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), a method that authorizes experience reuse before weight-changing training. BCIT binds an observed effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, and obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial when needed. Fully trained candidates still face a shared adoption rule, and only observed events extend memory. On one 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL, and function calling, candidate updates exhibit heterogeneous target and retention effects across the evaluated contexts. Under matched candidates, evidence, and compute, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and attains higher equal-budget final-model quality than the evaluated alternatives. These results support treating experience authorization as a distinct problem in autonomous post-training.

summary.takeaway: BCIT reduces wasted compute by conditioning reuse of past updates on source context, improving final model quality.
summary.problem: Autonomous LLM post‑training must decide when historical update evidence remains valid after the parent model changes.
summary.method: BCIT records source context, evidence, applicability rules, and hard conflicts, then rejects, validates via a bounded trial, or fully trains candidates.
summary.evidence: On a 4B model across three tasks, BCIT cuts harmful authorizations from 62.5% to 25.0% and achieves higher cross‑task mean under equal compute.
summary.limitations: Experiments cover only one 4B model, three capabilities, a single retention benchmark, and manually set boundaries.
summary.why_for_you: If you aim to make adversarial or efficient LLM training more compute‑aware, BCIT’s conditional reuse directly addresses wasteful update allocation.

signals.text: BCIT frames conditional experience transfer, cutting harmful update authorizations from 62.5% to 25.0%.
BCIT binds observed effects to source context, checks applicability, vetoes hard conflicts, and runs bounded trials before full training.
BCIT authorizes 2/8 harmful vs 5/8 baseline and yields higher cross‑task mean, evaluated on one 4B model.

deep_dive.overview: The paper defines conditional experience transfer, the problem of reusing past post‑training updates when the parent LLM has changed. It proposes Boundary‑Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT), which records each update’s source context, observed gain, applicability conditions, and named hard conflicts. At decision time BCIT either rejects a candidate, runs a short bounded trial on the current parent, or grants full training under a frozen rule, after which a shared adoption rule decides promotion. Experiments on a 4B model across finance reasoning, text‑to‑SQL, and function calling show BCIT reduces harmful authorizations and improves overall task performance under equal compute budgets.

methodology.title: Source‑bound record
methodology.detail: Each historical update is stored as (i, xs, Es, Bi, ρi) capturing the update, source context, observed evidence, applicability conditions, and conflict specifications.

methodology.title: Decision actions
methodology.detail: Given a candidate and current context, BCIT either rejects (hard conflict), validates via a bounded training trial (unresolved evidence), or authorizes full training (frozen rule).

methodology.title: Shared adoption rule
methodology.detail: All fully trained children are later evaluated with the same promote‑or‑rollback criterion, decoupling authorization from final selection.

mechanism.title: Context binding
mechanism.detail: Observed gains are tied to the exact parent model, data mixture, training stage, and evaluation protocol, preventing context‑free reuse.

mechanism.title: Applicability checking
mechanism.detail: Pre‑specified conditions (e.g., data domain, training stage) are evaluated; violations trigger vetoes or bounded trials.

experiments.title: Setup
experiments.detail: A 4B LLM adapted sequentially to three capabilities (finance reasoning, text‑to‑SQL, function calling). Candidates were matched on parent, seed, data scale, and budget.

experiments.title: Baselines
experiments.detail: Compared BCIT against Flat‑Additive, ValidateAll, and Additive+Veto policies using six seeds and equal GPU‑hour budgets.

experiments.title: Metrics
experiments.detail: Target task accuracy, two retention measures (IFEval‑P/I), harmful‑candidate authorization rate, beneficial‑candidate coverage, and cross‑task mean score.

findings.title: Harm reduction
findings.detail: BCIT authorized 2 of 8 harmful candidates (25.0%) versus 5 of 8 (62.5%) for Flat‑Additive.

findings.title: Beneficial retention
findings.detail: BCIT retained 9 of 10 beneficial candidates (90.0%) compared to 8 of 10 (80.0%) for the baseline.

findings.title: Overall performance
findings.detail: Under matched compute, BCIT achieved a higher cross‑task mean than all evaluated shared‑model alternatives.

contributions: Formulation of conditional experience transfer as a control problem in autonomous LLM post‑training.
Design of BCIT, a transparent reject‑validate‑train pipeline with explicit context binding and conflict vetoes.
Empirical evidence chain showing heterogeneous update effects and BCIT’s advantage in reducing harmful updates while preserving benefits.
limitations: Evidence limited to a single 4B model and three target tasks.
Only one retention benchmark and manually defined applicability boundaries were used.
Studies share candidates and are not independent replications; component analyses are descriptive rather than fully isolated.
open_questions: How does BCIT scale to larger models (e.g., 70B) and longer adaptation trajectories?
Can applicability conditions and conflict boundaries be learned automatically rather than hand‑specified?
What is the impact of BCIT on adversarial robustness and loss‑landscape geometry during sequential fine‑tuning?

papers.title: JudgeStealer: Extracting LLM Judging Capabilities across Evaluation Protocols
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used across various evaluation scenarios, making their judgment capabilities valuable intellectual property. However, black-box access exposes these capabilities to model extraction attacks. Existing extraction methods do not specifically target LLM judges and provide limited support for multiple evaluation protocols under restricted query budgets. In this study, we propose JUDGESTEALER, the first query-efficient model extraction framework for replicating judging capabilities across pointwise scoring, pairwise comparison, and listwise ranking protocols. JUDGESTEALER exploits the strong cross-protocol agreement to acquire pointwise scores and transform them into pairwise and listwise supervisions without additional victim queries. To capture informative judge patterns and improve query efficiency, JUDGESTEALER dynamically selects pointwise inputs based on semantic diversity, predictive uncertainty, and potential judge biases. It further applies score smoothing and multi-protocol review to preserve the ordinal structure of scores and mitigate catastrophic forgetting during surrogate adaptation. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLM-as-a-judge and reward models show that JUDGESTEALER consistently outperforms existing extraction baselines, achieving up to 73.3%, 87.0%, and 71.6% accuracy for pointwise, pairwise, and listwise evaluation, respectively. JUDGESTEALER also remains effective across different sur- rogate model scales, adaptation strategies, and reasoning settings. Moreover, JUDGESTEALER demonstrates robustness against representative extraction defenses.

summary.takeaway: JudgeStealer efficiently extracts LLM judging behavior across pointwise, pairwise, and listwise protocols using a two‑stage surrogate training pipeline.
summary.problem: Black‑box LLM judges can be stolen, yet existing extraction attacks lack support for multiple evaluation protocols under limited query budgets.
summary.method: The framework dynamically selects informative inputs via semantic diversity, predictive uncertainty, and bias signals, then applies adaptive score smoothing and multi‑protocol consolidation to train a surrogate judge.
summary.evidence: It attains up to 73.3% pointwise, 87.0% pairwise, and 71.6% listwise accuracy while remaining robust to representative defenses.
summary.limitations: Authors do not state explicit limitations.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant to your interest in efficient adversarial training because it demonstrates a query‑efficient attack that probes LLM loss landscapes across evaluation protocols.

signals.text: First framework to extract LLM judging capabilities across pointwise, pairwise, and listwise protocols
Dynamically selects inputs using semantic diversity, uncertainty, and bias, then smooths scores and consolidates multi‑protocol supervision
Achieves up to 73.3% pointwise, 87.0% pairwise, 71.6% listwise accuracy under ~600 queries

deep_dive.overview: JudgeStealer introduces a query‑efficient extraction pipeline that first gathers pointwise scores from a black‑box LLM judge, using a dynamic selection mechanism based on semantic diversity, predictive uncertainty, and potential judge bias. These scores are smoothed with an adaptive discrete Gaussian and used to warm‑up a surrogate model. In a second stage, the pointwise scores are transformed into pairwise and listwise supervision, and all three forms are jointly fine‑tuned, preserving ordinal structure and mitigating forgetting. Experiments on proprietary and open‑source judges show high accuracy across protocols and resilience to defenses.

methodology.title: Stage I – Pointwise Score Extraction
methodology.detail: Iteratively query the victim judge, select inputs via D, U, B signals, and train the surrogate with adaptive Gaussian‑smoothed cross‑entropy loss.

methodology.title: Stage II – Multi‑Protocol Extension
methodology.detail: Transform collected pointwise scores into pairwise comparisons and listwise rankings, then consolidate all supervision for joint surrogate adaptation.

mechanism.title: Cross‑Protocol Agreement Exploitation
mechanism.detail: Assumes strong agreement among pointwise, pairwise, and listwise judgments, allowing conversion of pointwise outputs into other protocol labels without extra victim queries.

mechanism.title: Dynamic Input Selection
mechanism.detail: Combines semantic diversity (D), predictive uncertainty (U), and bias estimation (B) to prioritize queries that reveal informative judge patterns.

mechanism.title: Adaptive Score Smoothing
mechanism.detail: Blends one‑hot targets with a trainable discrete Gaussian distribution to encode ordinal relationships and reduce catastrophic forgetting.

experiments.title: Evaluation Setup
experiments.detail: Surrogate: Qwen3‑1.7B (and others); Victims: GPT‑5.4, Llama‑3.2‑1B, Qwen3‑1.7B; Baselines: prior extraction attacks (KnockoffNet, Activethief, etc.); Metrics: Acc, Acc±1, MAE for each protocol; Query budget ≈600.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Removing any of D, U, B degrades performance; adaptive smoothing outperforms fixed smoothing and one‑hot supervision; consolidation stage contributes most runtime.

findings.title: Extraction Performance
findings.detail: JudgeStealer reaches 73.3% pointwise, 87.0% pairwise, and 71.6% listwise accuracy, surpassing all listed baselines.

findings.title: Robustness to Defenses
findings.detail: Maintains high accuracy against anomaly detection and ownership‑tracing defenses (e.g., Table 10 results).

findings.title: Efficiency
findings.detail: Full pipeline completes in 65 min 34 s for 600 queries; selection accounts for 23% of runtime.

contributions: First model extraction framework for LLM judges across multiple evaluation protocols
Query‑efficient dynamic input selection using diversity, uncertainty, and bias signals
Adaptive score smoothing and multi‑protocol consolidation preserving ordinal structure
limitations: No explicit limitation discussion; evaluation limited to specific victim models and a ~600‑query budget
open_questions: How does the approach scale to larger query budgets or more restrictive API limits?
Can adaptive defenses that modify output distributions undermine the cross‑protocol transformation?
Is the method applicable to extracting other LLM functionalities beyond judging?

papers.title: Surgical Alignment in Knowledge Graph Training for Clinical Diagnosis with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) offer structured medical knowledge that can ground large language model (LLM) reasoning in clinical diagnosis application, yet how KG signal should be integrated into LLMs remains an open question. We present a systematic study spanning five KG task formulations, three training paradigms, two KGs, and three base LLMs. At the task level, all paradigms improve over the non-finetuned baseline, but methods with comparable in-domain accuracy show substantially different knowledge transfer behavior. We introduce Gradient Intervention Density (GID) and Gradient Distortion (GD) to measure how broadly an optimizer modifies the pretrained model. GID and GD together reveal a clear divide: KG-judgment training under KL regularization produces sparse, localized updates (a regime we term as surgical alignment), while task-specific SFT produces dense ones. A controlled ablation shows that the objective and KL contribute to sparsity independently, and the paradigms that produce sparse updates also improve reasoning quality, even when their in-domain accuracy is lower than task-specific SFT. Assessing KG-LLM integration thus requires complementing accuracy with optimization-geometry diagnostics. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/LARK-NLP-Lab/Surgical-Alignment.

summary.takeaway: We present a systematic study spanning five KG task formulations, three training paradigms, two KGs, and three base LLMs.
summary.problem: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) offer structured medical knowledge that can ground large language model (LLM) reasoning in clinical diagnosis application, yet how KG signal should be integrated into LLMs remains an open question.
summary.method: We introduce Gradient Intervention Density (GID) and Gradient Distortion (GD) to measure how broadly an optimizer modifies the pretrained model.
summary.evidence: At the task level, all paradigms improve over the non-finetuned baseline, but methods with comparable in-domain accuracy show substantially different knowledge transfer behavior.

papers.title: Robust CurveMoE: Multi-Norm Adversarial Defense for Mixture-of-Experts Models via Mode Connectivity
papers.abstract: Multi-norm adversarial defense aims to protect neural networks against perturbations defined by different norm constraints, but existing methods typically optimize competing robustness objectives within a single parameter configuration, leading to substantial training cost and unfavorable robustness trade-offs. We propose Robust CurveMoE, an efficient mixture-of-experts framework that connects models specialized for different perturbation norms through a low-loss path and exploits the complementary robustness profiles of models along this path. Robust CurveMoE derives clean and norm-specialized experts from robustness-constrained curve locations and selectively expertizes only influential layers, while sharing the remaining parameters across routing paths. To further reduce curve-construction cost, we introduce contribution-guided partial updating, which selects influential curve parameters using initialization-based gradient scores. We also theoretically bound the objective gap between partial and full curve optimization. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 with WideResNet and Vision Transformer architectures show that Robust CurveMoE consistently improves clean, norm-specific, and Union accuracy over MSD and ERMC. In particular, it improves Union accuracy by 2.37 and 2.13 percentage points over the strongest baseline on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100, respectively. Extensive ablations further validate the effectiveness of partial updating, selective expertization, and robustness-constrained expert selection.

summary.takeaway: We propose Robust CurveMoE, an efficient mixture-of-experts framework that connects models specialized for different perturbation norms through a low-loss path and exploits the complementary robustness profiles of models along this path.
summary.problem: Multi-norm adversarial defense aims to protect neural networks against perturbations defined by different norm constraints, but existing methods typically optimize competing robustness objectives within a single parameter configuration, leading to substantial training cost and unfavorable robustness trade-offs.
summary.method: We propose Robust CurveMoE, an efficient mixture-of-experts framework that connects models specialized for different perturbation norms through a low-loss path and exploits the complementary robustness profiles of models along this path.

papers.title: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update's forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

summary.why_for_you: 高效对抗训练专家会看重 FRAG 的 training-free 对齐指标，用于在无需重新学习攻击的情况下评估忘记鲁棒性。
summary.limitations: FRAG 需要校准数据，且主要在 transformer 架构上进行评估。

summary.evidence: 在多种忘记方法和模型中，FRAG 与实际重新学习鲁棒性的相关性比全局距离更可靠。
summary.takeaway: FRAG 与 FRP 通过优先考虑忘记-保留对齐而非全局距离，提升重新学习鲁棒性。

papers.title: Are LLM-Enhanced GNNs Privacy-Safe?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently advanced graph neural networks (GNNs) by enriching node representations with semantic information, giving rise to LLM-enhanced GNNs that achieve substantial performance gains. However, their vulnerability to privacy attacks, in which adversaries infer sensitive information from model outputs, remains largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic evaluation of privacy risks in LLM-enhanced GNNs through a unified framework consisting of five stages: (1) dataset preparation, (2) victim model training, (3) privacy attack, (4) risk assessment, and (5) defense analysis. Specifically, we conduct experiments on six real-world text-attributed graph datasets covering diverse domains. We consider six representative privacy attack methods targeting three fundamental threats, namely link, label, and membership inference, and construct 42 victim model configurations by combining multiple LLM-based feature enhancers with representative GNN backbones. Extensive experiments show that, despite their utility improvements, LLM-enhanced GNNs consistently exhibit increased vulnerability to privacy attacks compared to shallow text representation baselines. Further analysis reveals that semantic enrichment amplifies link-, label-, and membership-related signals in the embedding space, making them more exploitable by inference attacks. Finally, we evaluate differential privacy as a defense strategy and show that, while it can partially mitigate privacy risks, it introduces significant utility degradation, highlighting a fundamental privacy-utility trade-off in LLM-enhanced graph learning. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of privacy risks in LLM-enhanced GNNs and offers practical insights for developing more secure and trustworthy graph learning systems.

summary.takeaway: LLM‑增强的 GNN 在提升节点分类准确率的同时，会显著增加对链接、标签和成员推断攻击的易感性，差分隐私只能在高代价的实用性损失下部分缓解。

summary.evidence: 大量实验表明，LLM‑增强的 GNN 相较于浅层基线泄露更多隐私，使用差分隐私可降低泄露但会显著下降分类准确率。

papers.title: Making Clinical Language Models Auditable: Concept-Guided Fine-Tuning for Robust Prediction
papers.abstract: Clinical language models can achieve strong in-hospital accuracy yet fail under deployment shifts because they exploit note-specific artifacts (e.g., templates, separators, boilerplate) that do not reflect patient state. We propose CAST (Concept-guided Artifact Suppression Tuning), an SAE-based framework for auditable clinical text classification. CAST uses Sparse Autoencoders to expose sparse, human-auditable features from intermediate Transformer activations, labels SAE latents with an LLM-assisted interpretation pipeline and ICD-10 retrieval constraints, suppresses verified artifact latents via residual subtraction during fine-tuning, and provides post-hoc per-concept attributions for auditing model decisions. On MIMIC-IV discharge-note mortality prediction, CAST improves over its corresponding fine-tuned encoder baselines and remains competitive with strong LLM baselines, while producing a feature-level audit trail of the clinical concepts that support each prediction and the artifact concepts suppressed during training.

summary.takeaway: We propose CAST (Concept-guided Artifact Suppression Tuning), an SAE-based framework for auditable clinical text classification.
summary.problem: Clinical language models can achieve strong in-hospital accuracy yet fail under deployment shifts because they exploit note-specific artifacts (e.g., templates, separators, boilerplate) that do not reflect patient state.
summary.method: We propose CAST (Concept-guided Artifact Suppression Tuning), an SAE-based framework for auditable clinical text classification.
summary.evidence: On MIMIC-IV discharge-note mortality prediction, CAST improves over its corresponding fine-tuned encoder baselines and remains competitive with strong LLM baselines, while producing a feature-level audit trail of the clinical concepts that support each prediction and the artifact concepts suppressed during training.

papers.title: A Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Framework Defense against LLM Jailbreak Attacks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit techniques such as role-playing, obfuscation, code transformation, and multi-step indirection to elicit harmful outputs. As jailbreak strategies keep emerging, defenses have proliferated in an ongoing cat-and-mouse game, yet most remain static: their safety behavior is fixed at deployment, so they cannot accumulate defensive experience or adapt to unseen strategies. We propose a self-evolving test-time defense built around a persistent, cross-interaction rule memory: when an attack succeeds, the framework abstracts that failure into a method-level rule capturing the structural attack wrapper rather than the harmful topic, and reuses it against future inputs. Because rules are method-level, one induced rule generalizes across an entire attack family, and the label space expands as novel wrappers appear. The mechanism operates entirely through external memory and prompting, with no parameter updates, and applies to both open-weight and black-box API models. We realize it as four cooperating modules, but the contribution is the memory-based adaptation mechanism, not the module decomposition. Across four black-box jailbreak families and multiple models, our method substantially reduces attack success rates while preserving benign utility, remains robust under an adaptive composite-wrapper attack, and does not increase over-refusal as the memory grows.

summary.takeaway: 一种基于记忆的测试时防御，能够从 jailbreak 失败中学习，在不修改模型参数的情况下显著降低攻击成功率。

deep_dive.overview: 本文提出一种自演化的 test‑time 防御，将 method‑level 规则存储在外部记忆中。当 jailbreak 成功时，reflection 代理将结构化包装抽象为规则，triggering 代理据此检测未来相似输入。policy 代理根据匹配规则执行硬拒或软拒，response 代理生成最终输出。模型参数不被修改，可部署于 open‑weight 与 black‑box LLM API。

papers.title: SPT: Skills as Pre-Training Data for Agentic Language Models
papers.abstract: Agentic (tool-using) language models are mainly trained on tool-call traces and agent trajectories during post-training. These data provide direct behavioral supervision, but producing them requires task environments, execution, and verification, making broad tool and task coverage expensive. Publicly available skills offer another source of training data: they encode reusable tool semantics and workflows but are typically used only as inference-time context. We introduce Skill Pre-Training (SPT), a mid-training method that applies causal language modeling to SkillCorpus, a collection of public multi-file skill packages, optionally mixed with general data. To preserve relations among files within each package, we also introduce Reference Insert, a reference-aware assembly strategy that places supporting files near their mentions in the primary instruction. Experiments across multiple model scales and post-training recipes show that SPT consistently improves agentic performance over mid-training on general or trajectory data, while largely preserving general performance. Data mixture experiments show additional benefits from combining skill data with general annealing corpora. These results indicate that skill packages are a valuable data source for pre-training agentic language models.

papers.title: From Passive Response to Proactive Correction: Enhancing LLM Robustness Against Input Fact Perturbations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently produce confident yet factually incorrect responses when user inputs contain misleading premises, a phenomenon we attribute to fact perturbations in the input. Existing approaches to hallucination mitigation typically assume reliable user inputs, overlooking how such factual errors can actively mislead model reasoning. To address this vulnerability, we propose DEDUCE, a three-stage framework that transforms LLMs from passive responders into proactive error correctors. DEDUCE operates in three stages: (1) detect errors through fine-grained fact extraction and verification; (2) devise correction strategies via multi perspective deliberation; and (3) correct misconceptions while delivering reliable answers. We also present MisFactQA, a dataset containing factual errors of varying degrees, and propose new metrics for evaluating model robustness. Experiments on TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and our MisFactQA benchmark demonstrate that DEDUCE significantly improves both accuracy and error correction capability. Consistent gains across Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma families confirm its effectiveness and scalability.
papers.comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026

summary.takeaway: DEDUCE converts LLMs from passive responders into proactive correctors of fact‑perturbed inputs, markedly boosting robustness.
summary.problem: User queries often contain factual errors that mislead LLM reasoning and cause hallucinations.
summary.method: A three‑stage framework (detect, devise, correct) extracts fine‑grained facts, deliberates multi‑perspective correction strategies, and generates clarified answers.
summary.evidence: Across Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma models, DEDUCE raises accuracy up to 25.99% on FalseQA and improves correction and clarification scores while lowering misleading rates.

summary.why_for_you: Matches your interest in trustworthy LLMs by directly tackling input‑induced hallucinations and offering new robustness metrics.

deep_dive.overview: The paper identifies input fact perturbations as a major source of LLM hallucinations and proposes DEDUCE, a three‑stage pipeline that first detects erroneous factual units via fine‑grained extraction and verification, then generates correction strategies through multi‑perspective deliberation, and finally produces clarified answers. A new benchmark, MisFactQA, and three robustness metrics (Misleading Rate, Correction Rate, Clarification Score) are introduced. Experiments on TruthfulQA, FalseQA, and MisFactQA with Qwen, LLaMA, and Gemma families show consistent accuracy gains, higher correction rates, and reduced misleading behavior, demonstrating scalability of the approach.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Bias Inheritance in LLM-based Data Augmentation on Downstream Tasks
papers.abstract: Generating synthetic datasets via large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising approach to improve LLM performance. However, LLMs inherently reflect biases in their training data, leading to a critical challenge: when models are trained on synthetic data, they may propagate and amplify the inherent biases that can significantly impact fairness and robustness on downstream tasks—a phenomenon we term bias inheritance. This work presents the first systematic investigation in understanding, analyzing, and mitigating bias inheritance. We fine-tune LLMs with a combined dataset of real and LLM-augmented data with varied bias ratio as the proportion of augmented data. Through systematic experiments across 10 classification and generation tasks, we analyze how 6 different types of biases manifest. Our results indicate that bias inheritance harms downstream task performance in bias directly-related classification and generation tasks. Then, our analysis identifies three key misalignment factors: misalignment of values, group data, and data distributions. Based on these insights, we propose three mitigation strategies: token-based, mask-based, and loss-based approaches, which can work differently on various tasks and bias, indicating the substantial challenges to mitigate bias inheritance. We hope this work can provide insights to the research of LLM data augmentation.

papers.title: User Perceptions vs. Proxy LLM Judges: Privacy and Helpfulness in LLM Responses to Privacy-Sensitive Scenarios
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being adopted for tasks like drafting emails, summarizing meetings, and answering health questions. In these settings, users may need to share private information (e.g., contact details, health records). To evaluate LLMs' ability to identify and redact such information, prior work introduced real-life, scenario-based benchmarks (e.g., ConfAIde, PrivacyLens) and found that LLMs can leak private information in complex scenarios. However, these evaluations relied on proxy LLMs to judge the helpfulness and privacy-preservation quality of LLM responses, rather than directly measuring users' perceptions. To understand how users perceive the helpfulness and privacy-preservation quality of LLM responses to privacy-sensitive scenarios, we conducted a user study ($n=94$) using 90 PrivacyLens scenarios. We found that users had low agreement with each other when evaluating identical LLM responses. In contrast, five proxy LLMs reached high agreement, yet each proxy LLM had low correlation with users' evaluations. These results indicate that proxy LLMs cannot accurately estimate users' wide range of perceptions of utility and privacy in privacy-sensitive scenarios. We discuss the need for more user-centered studies to measure LLMs' ability to help users while preserving privacy, and for improving alignment between LLMs and users in estimating perceived privacy and utility.

papers.title: OPUS: Towards Efficient and Principled Data Selection in Large Language Model Pre-training in Every Iteration
papers.abstract: As high-quality public text approaches exhaustion, a phenomenon known as the Data Wall—LLM pre-training is shifting from more tokens to better tokens. However, existing methods either rely on heuristic static filters that ignore training dynamics, or use dynamic yet optimizer-agnostic criteria based on raw gradients. We propose OPUS (Optimizer-induced Projected Utility Selection), a dynamic framework that defines utility in the optimizer-induced update space. OPUS scores candidates by projecting their effective updates, shaped by modern optimizers, onto a target direction derived from a stable, in-distribution proxy. To ensure scalability, we employ Ghost technique with CountSketch for computational efficiency, and Boltzmann sampling for data diversity, incurring only 4.7% additional compute overhead. OPUS achieves remarkable results across diverse corpora, quality tiers, optimizers, and model scales. It also outperforms previous data selection methods across different stages of training, including from-scratch pre-training and also mid-training. Beyond online selection, the OPUS utility score also demonstrates potential as a static filter for flagging and removing toxic documents from contaminated training corpora prior to training.

summary.takeaway: OPUS 通过将 optimizer‑induced 更新投影到 target direction，高效选择更高效用的训练标记。

deep_dive.overview: OPUS 通过在 optimizer‑induced 更新空间定义效用来应对 Data Wall。它利用现代优化器计算的有效更新，将其投影到由稳定分布代理得到的 target direction 上，为每个候选标记计算效用分数。通过 Ghost 技术结合 CountSketch 实现可扩展性，并使用 Boltzmann 采样保持数据多样性。跨不同语料库、质量层级、optimizers 和模型规模的实验表明，相比现有静态和动态选择方法，OPUS 能持续提升性能，且仅带来约 4.7% 的计算增量。该效用分数亦可用作有害数据的静态过滤器。

papers.title: A Goal Without a Plan Is Just a Wish: Efficient and Effective Global Planner Training for Long-Horizon Agent Task
papers.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) struggle with brainless trial-and-error and generating hallucinatory actions due to a lack of global planning in long-horizon tasks. In this paper, we introduce a plan-and-execute framework and propose EAGLET, an efficient and effective planner training method to enhance the executor agent's planning abilities without human effort. Specifically, we train a plug-and-play global planner through a two-step process: we first synthesize high-quality plans from an advanced LLM using our proposed homologous consensus filtering strategy, and apply fine-tuning as a cold start. Moreover, we further improve the planner with a rule-based reinforcement learning stage using a novel executor capability gain reward, ensuring it can handle task instructions of varying difficulty. Experiments on three long-horizon agent tasks show that executor agents equipped with our planner outperform existing methods, achieving new state-of-the-art performance. Meanwhile, EAGLET reduces training costs by 8× compared to RL-based baselines, and it does not require manual effort or extra training data, offering an efficient and effective solution.
